items.title: Hemodynamic criteria for cardiogenic shock
items.contentHtml:
Definition and criteria

  • Cardiogenic shock is a state of tissue hypoperfusion due to insufficient cardiac output despite adequate intravascular volume.
  • Classical criteria (SHOCK trials): systolic blood pressure <90 mmHg for ≥30 minutes or need for vasopressors to maintain it, with cardiac rate <2.2 L/min/m² and pulmonary wedge pressure >15 mmHg.
  • Current definition (SCAI 2019): stages A–E; established shock corresponds to stage C (hypoperfusion requiring intervention) and stage D (refractory).
  • The mean arterial pressure is not part of the diagnostic criteria, but is a therapeutic objective.

items.title: Acute myocardial infarction as the main cause
items.contentHtml:
Acute myocardial infarction (AMI)

  • The most common cause is acute myocardial infarction (AMI), especially with anterior ST segment elevation (STEMI).
  • Acute left ventricular dysfunction due to loss of myocardium >40% of the left ventricle usually precipitates shock.
  • Mechanical complications of the AMI (free wall rupture, interventricular septum rupture, acute mitral regurgitation due to papillary muscle rupture) are secondary causes that require urgent surgery.
  • The diagnosis is confirmed with electrocardiogram (ST elevation) and biomarkers (elevated troponin).
  • Early reperfusion is the mainstay of treatment (see specific focus).

items.title: Cardiogenic vs obstructive shock
items.contentHtml:
Key differences

  • In cardiogenic shock the problem is pump failure (decreased contractility or filling due to intrinsic cardiac cause).
  • In obstructive shock there is a mechanical obstruction to blood flow, with low cardiac output but intrinsically normal myocardial function.
  • Causes of obstructive: massive pulmonary thromboembolism, cardiac tamponade, tension pneumothorax, critical aortic stenosis.
  • Echocardiography is essential: in cardiogenic, diffuse or segmental hypokinesia is seen; In the obstructive, pericardial effusion is seen, signs of right overload or left ventricular hypertrophy with aortic gradient.
  • The treatment of the obstructive is specific (pericardiocentesis, thrombolysis, etc.), not inotropic as a first line.

items.title: Recognize hypoperfusion
items.contentHtml:
Clinical and laboratory signs

  • Cutaneous hypoperfusion: cold, pale, sweaty skin, with capillary refilling >3 seconds.
  • Altered mental status: confusion, agitation or drowsiness.
  • Oliguria: diuresis <0.5 mL/kg/hour for at least 2 hours.
  • Laboratory: elevated serum lactate (>2 mmol/L), negative base deficiency in blood gas, increased creatinine, elevated transaminases due to hepatic congestion.
  • The presence of hypoperfusion distinguishes shock from isolated hypotension.

items.title: Mean blood pressure goal
items.contentHtml:
Target mean arterial pressure (MAP)

  • Initial goal mean arterial pressure (MAP) ≥65 mmHg in most patients with cardiogenic shock.
  • In patients with chronic arterial hypertension or aortic stenosis, a higher MAP (70–75) may be required. mmHg) to maintain coronary and cerebral perfusion.
  • MAP is calculated as: MAP = (systolic blood pressure + 2 × diastolic blood pressure) / 3.
  • Invasive monitoring with arterial catheter is preferred for continuous adjustment.
  • Target MAP should be adjusted according to perfusion markers (lactate, urine output, mental status).

items.title: Norepinephrine and other agents
items.contentHtml:
Inotropes and vasopressors

  • Norepinephrine is the first-line vasopressor in cardiogenic shock, at doses of 0.05–0.5 µg/kg/min, due to its alpha and beta profile.
  • Dobutamine (inotrope) is added if there is low cardiac output with adequate blood pressure or as an adjuvant to norepinephrine; dose 2.5–10 µg/kg/min.
  • Epinephrine is reserved for refractory cases or cardiac arrest, not as first line.
  • Levosimendan (calcium sensitizer) is an alternative in patients with beta-blockers or diastolic dysfunction.
  • Avoid norepinephrine in high doses without inotrope if there is very low cardiac output so as not to increase afterload excessively.

items.title: Intra-aortic balloon pump (IABP)
items.contentHtml:
Intra-aortic balloon pump (IABP)

  • The intra-aortic balloon pump (IABP) is a percutaneous device that is placed in the descending aorta and inflates in diastole, increasing coronary diastolic pressure and myocardial perfusion.
  • It deflates. in systole, reducing afterload and ventricular work.
  • Indicated in cardiogenic shock due to acute myocardial infarction with mechanical complications (mitral regurgitation, ventricular septal defect) or as a bridge to revascularization.
  • It has not been shown to reduce mortality in the IABP-SHOCK II trial as routine use; Its use is selective.
  • Contraindications: moderate/severe aortic insufficiency, aortic dissection, severe peripheral vascular disease, coagulopathy.

items.title: Asistencia ventricular mecánica
items.contentHtml:
Circulatory support devices

  • Ventricular assist devices (VAD) are used in cardiogenic shock refractory to drugs and balloon.
  • Impella (percutaneous axial pump) provides flow of up to 5 L/min (Impella 5.0), unloading the left ventricle and improving perfusion coronary.
  • Extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO) Venoarterial (VA-ECMO) offers complete cardiopulmonary support; is considered to be in arrest or very severe shock.
  • The choice depends on availability, cause and neurological prognosis.
  • Complications: hemolysis, thrombosis, bleeding, infection.
  • The heart transplant or artificial ventricle are long-term options.

items.title: Estenosis aórtica crítica: contraindicaciones
items.contentHtml:
Estenosis aórtica crítica

  • La estenosis aórtica crítica (área valvular <1,0 cm²) es contraindicación relativa para el uso de balón de contrapulsación intraaórtico (BCIA) porque la reducción de la poscarga no beneficia y puede causar hipotensión severa.
  • También contraindica el uso de Impella (el catéter no puede cruzar la válvula estenótica sin riesgo de daño).
  • En shock cardiogénico por estenosis aórtica (p. ej., tras reemplazo valvular fallido), el tratamiento es quirúrgico o valvuloplastia aórtica percutánea urgente.
  • Los vasodilatadores (nitroprusiato) están contraindicados porque disminuyen la presión de perfusión coronaria.
  • La noradrenalina puede usarse para mantener la presión arterial media, pero no corrige el obstáculo.

items.title: Early reperfusion in AMI
items.contentHtml:
Early reperfusion

  • In cardiogenic shock from acute myocardial infarction (AMI), early reperfusion is the most important treatment, with primary percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) within the first 2 hours of diagnosis if possible.
  • The SHOCK trial demonstrated that early revascularization (PCI or surgery) reduces mortality at 6 months compared to initial medical treatment.
  • Fibrinolysis is contraindicated in cardiogenic shock if there is no access to immediate PCI; PCI is preferred.
  • If PCI is not feasible, urgent revascularization surgery is considered.
  • Circulatory support with intra-aortic balloon pump or Impella may be initiated before PCI if there is extreme instability.

items.title: Liquid management and monitoring
items.contentHtml:
Fluids in cardiogenic shock

  • Most patients have pulmonary congestion and elevated pulmonary wedge pressure; therefore, fluid administration should be restricted and diuretics (intravenous furosemide) should be used if there is overload. Crystalloid boluses (250–500 mL) are only administered if there are signs of hypovolemia (low central venous pressure, previous volume response). Pulmonary artery can guide filling, but does not improve survival in routine use.
  • Serial echocardiography is preferred to evaluate intravascular volume and contractility.
  • The goal is to maintain mean arterial pressure ≥65 mmHg with the least amount of volume possible.

items.title: Prognosis and mortality
items.contentHtml:
Prognosis

  • Mortality from cardiogenic shock remains high, between 40–50% at 30 days in recent trials.
  • Mortality is higher if there is previous cardiac arrest, lactate >10 mmol/L, kidney dysfunction or age
  • Evaluation with the SCAI scale (stage E) predicts mortality almost 100% without advanced support.
